claims.text: Superconducting transition temperature in high-entropy alloys is primarily determined by average valence electron concentration.
Average valence electron concentration governs the density of states at the Fermi level.
The density of states at the Fermi level modulates electron–phonon coupling strength within a BCS framework.
The baseline material is a single-phase solid solution containing at least five elements at concentrations of at least 5 at% each.
The comparison can hold atomic-size dispersity and noncomposition entropy contributions approximately fixed.
Composition can be varied to change VEC while atomic-size differences, lattice distortion, and other structural parameters remain approximately constant.
Maintaining a single phase and identical processing minimizes confounding from disorder and microstructural changes.
Changes in VEC modify the density of states at the Fermi level, which mediates their effect on electron–phonon coupling.
Adjusting VEC shifts the Fermi level relative to peaks in the electronic density of states.
A VEC-induced change in the density of states alters the electron–phonon coupling constant.
Changes in electron–phonon coupling modulate Tc according to classical BCS/McMillan theory.
Systematic variation of VEC will produce correlated changes in the density of states at the Fermi level and in Tc.
An optimal VEC that places the Fermi level at a density-of-states peak will enhance Tc relative to the baseline.
The starting HEA has Tc and electron–phonon coupling comparable to known Nb–Ta-based HEAs.
Known Nb–Ta-based HEAs have an electron–phonon coupling constant of approximately 0.7.
The studied HEA evidence is consistent with bulk, near-BCS-type superconductivity and a measurable density of states at the Fermi level.
The proposed VEC-controlled relationship applies only while the alloys remain single-phase solid solutions with approximately constant disorder and atomic-size dispersity.
Phase separation or processing-induced structural changes could invalidate attribution of Tc changes to VEC.
Minor variations in local atomic configurations and disorder may prevent a unique quantitative VEC–Tc relationship.
Failure of VEC variation to produce systematic correlated changes in both the Fermi-level density of states and Tc would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.
